title: Trump’s sneaky plan to gut Endangered Species Act draws from 1995 Scalia dissent
gist: A September 14, 2026 internal FWS memo reinterprets the Endangered Species Act to prohibit only intentional killing of animals, not incidental/accidental deaths from habitat destruction, effectively adopting Justice Scalia's 1995 dissenting view (which lost 6-3) as policy; advocates and legal scholars call it an unprecedented gutting of the ESA that is already drawing lawsuits from 21 state attorneys general.

themes.theme: The policy shift: from habitat protection to intent-only enforcement

insights.claim: A September 14, 2026 internal memo from FWS Director Brian Nesvik instructs field staff that the Endangered Species Act will now only prohibit actions 'specifically intending to target an animal,' rather than prohibiting habitat modifications that injure or accidentally kill protected species.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This is a material deregulatory shift for any industry (logging, real estate development, shipping, energy) whose operations incidentally affect protected species habitat, potentially removing a major compliance cost and permitting requirement.
insights.quote: A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it because the vessel's course was not set against the whale... Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.
insights.locator: FWS Director Brian Nesvik instructed staff in the September 14 memo

insights.claim: This memo follows an earlier 2026 rule change that already removed habitat destruction from the ESA's legal definition of 'harm,' which the administration justified as preventing extra costs to landowners; advocates say they were told at the time this would not be used to excuse preventable animal deaths, but the new memo does exactly that.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The two-step sequencing (redefine 'harm,' then reinterpret 'take') suggests a deliberate incremental deregulatory strategy that could be replicated in other environmental statutes, a pattern worth watching across agencies.
insights.quote: This is an incredibly sneaky and disingenuous way of going about things.
insights.locator: Ben Levitan, a senior attorney for legal conservation nonprofit Earthjustice

insights.claim: Incidental takings (accidental killings from habitat modification, not direct hunting) are described as the most common way endangered animals die, meaning the new intent-only standard is expected to gut most of the ESA's practical protective effect.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Because incidental takings are the dominant cause of protected-species deaths, this rule change has outsized real-world impact despite appearing narrow, a key point for assessing environmental-compliance risk reduction for land-use industries.
insights.locator: Such incidental takings are the most common way that endangered animals die

themes.theme: Legal foundation: reviving a 1995 Scalia dissent via Chevron's death

insights.claim: Trump's FWS policy is explicitly modeled on Justice Antonin Scalia's 1995 dissent in a Supreme Court case (Babbitt v. Sweet Home), which argued the ESA's 'take' provision applies only to intentional, direct acts against particular animals, not to population-level habitat protection; the administration believes the 1995 majority ruling was invalidated by the more recent death of the 'Chevron doctrine.'
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This is a textbook example of using the Supreme Court's Chevron reversal to relitigate settled regulatory interpretations decades later; investors in regulated industries (land use, energy, infrastructure) should expect more agencies to revisit old rules on similar legal grounds.
insights.locator: Trump is so intent on flipping the ESA that the dissent

insights.claim: The original 1995 case was decided 6-3 in favor of broad habitat protection, with the majority (opinion by Justice John Paul Stevens) basing its ruling on a textual reading finding Congress used 'the broadest possible terms' to define takings, specifically to include 'harassment, whether intentional or not' — meaning the current policy revives a losing minority legal position.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Because the administration's legal theory was explicitly the losing dissent (not the controlling precedent), legal experts see a strong likelihood of it being struck down again in court, an important variable for the durability of this deregulation.
insights.quote: Under the dissent's interpretation of the Act, a developer could drain a pond, knowing that the act would extinguish an endangered species of turtles, without even proposing a conservation plan or applying for a permit.
insights.locator: In the opinion drafted by late Justice John Paul Stevens

insights.claim: Justice Sandra Day O'Connor's 1995 concurrence, which Scalia mocked in a footnote as 'imaginative,' argued that destroying breeding habitat injures individual animals in the same way sterilization does, and could cause species extinction within a generation (citing the piping plover) — a framework the current FWS policy explicitly rejects.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: O'Connor's individual-injury-via-breeding-destruction framework is the doctrinal counter-argument likely to be central in upcoming litigation against the new FWS policy.
insights.quote: To raze the last remaining ground on which the piping plover currently breeds, thereby making it impossible for any piping plovers to reproduce, would obviously injure the population.
insights.locator: Saying that she didn't find it as "easy" as Scalia

insights.claim: The Trump administration already faces a lawsuit from a coalition of 21 state attorneys general over changes to the ESA, and legal experts including Harvard law professor Andrew Mergen call the new FWS memo 'an assault on the act like we've never seen before.'
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Active, well-resourced multi-state litigation makes near-term legal reversal plausible, meaning any compliance relief this policy offers to regulated industries may prove temporary.
insights.quote: What the administration is proposing to do is take all of the force out of what we have all understood the act to mean: Don't kill endangered species... What they seem to be saying in this document is 'it doesn't matter if you killed an endangered species if you didn't mean to.'
insights.locator: Andrew Mergen, a law professor at Harvard University

insights.claim: Vermont Law School emeritus professor Patrick Parenteau, who noted the 1995 majority ruled on textual grounds rather than agency-authority grounds (meaning Chevron's demise doesn't directly undermine it), expects the FWS will struggle to legally defend the new policy and flatly rejects the idea that the law is 'settled in favor of Scalia's dissent.'
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A textual (not deference-based) 1995 ruling being largely immune to the Chevron reversal is the key legal weakness in the administration's strategy, a specific angle likely to determine litigation outcomes.
insights.quote: To say that the law is settled in favor of Scalia's dissent? Absolutely not.
insights.locator: Parenteau, the Vermont law professor, told the Times
